title: Benjamin Logan
summary: In 1775 Benjamin Logan built Logan’s Station near present-day Stanford, held it through a 1777 siege, and later helped write Kentucky’s first constitution.
bodyMarkdown:
Benjamin Logan was one of the central figures of early Kentucky settlement. He founded one of its first stations, defended it through a long siege, and led militia campaigns against Shawnee towns north of the Ohio River. [A biography of Benjamin Logan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Logan) gives his birth date as May 1, 1743.

## From Virginia to Kentucky

Logan grew up in Virginia. He served on Col. Henry Bouquet's 1764 expedition and in Dunmore's War in 1774. In early 1775 he traveled to Kentucky with a party on the Wilderness Road.

Sources differ on the details. He left Daniel Boone's party. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker for Logan's Station](https://history.ky.gov/markers/logans-station) says he left Richard Henderson's party at Hazel Patch on April 15, 1775. Both agree he headed west and, according to the KHS marker, established his station on May 1, 1775, with John Floyd's help.

## Logan's Fort

The settlement grew up near Buffalo Spring and was also called St. Asaph. A [150-by-90-foot stockade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Stanford,_Kentucky) enclosed family cabins. A second KHS marker, on the [Wilderness Road at Logan's Station](https://history.ky.gov/markers/wilderness-roadlogans-station), notes the fort's place on the main route into Kentucky.

In May 1777, about 100 warriors besieged the fort. The siege lasted 13 days. Early in the fighting, Logan ran out under fire and carried the wounded Burr Harrison back inside. The Kentucky Heritage Council's [Logan's Fort page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Logan's-Fort.aspx) records that Harrison and William Hudson were killed, and that archaeologists found Hudson's remains in the 1990s.

With powder running low, Logan slipped out at night and traveled about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for more. He returned ahead of a relief party under John Bowman, which helped end the siege.

## Campaigns north of the Ohio

Logan was second in command on Bowman's 1779 raid on the Shawnee town of Chillicothe, told in [Col. John Bowman at Old Chillicothe](/stories/col-john-bowman-at-old-chillicothe/). In 1786 he led a larger campaign that burned thirteen Shawnee towns in present-day Ohio. During that raid, [Hugh McGary](/stories/hugh-mcgary-the-blue-licks-hothead/) killed the Shawnee leader Moluntha, who had come forward under a U.S. flag and had signed the Fort Finney treaty. That killing is told in [Moluntha and Logan's Raid](/stories/moluntha-and-logans-raid-1786/). The [Explore Kentucky History entry on Logan](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/572) summarizes his military and political career.

## Statehood and politics

Logan was a delegate to the 1792 convention that wrote Kentucky's first constitution. He ran for governor in 1795 and 1800 but lost both times. He died on December 11, 1802, at his home in Shelby County.

## Kentucky today

The site of Logan's Fort is in Stanford, the Lincoln County seat, told in [Stanford from St. Asaph](/stories/stanford-from-st-asaph/). Logan County in Kentucky and Logan County in Ohio are both named for him. His career reflects both sides of the frontier: the defense of a settler station and the destruction of Shawnee towns.
